setting: A criminal trial concerns a stolen camera. The defendant has offered no character evidence, and the prosecutor offers an unrelated past theft solely to suggest the defendant steals whenever possible.

transcript.speaker: Q
transcript.text: What did the defendant do at your shop three years ago?

transcript.speaker: A
transcript.text: He took a watch without paying.

explanation: The earlier theft is offered only to prove a propensity to steal and conduct in accordance with it.
trap_note: A prior act needs a permitted nonpropensity purpose, not just similarity in wrongdoing.

setting: A criminal trial concerns an alleged assault outside a diner. The defendant has not placed character in issue; the prosecutor offers general violent reputation to prove the charged act.

transcript.speaker: Q
transcript.text: What is the defendant's reputation for peacefulness?

transcript.speaker: A
transcript.text: People around our block call him a fighter.

explanation: The prosecution cannot use general violent character simply to prove the defendant committed this assault.
trap_note: A reputation format does not make an otherwise forbidden propensity use permissible.

setting: A civil trial concerns whether a driver ran a stop sign. Counsel offers a neighbor's account of the driver's general carelessness solely to prove careless driving on this occasion.

transcript.speaker: Q
transcript.text: What sort of person is the driver around the neighborhood?

transcript.speaker: A
transcript.text: Careless. He never seems to pay attention.

explanation: General character for carelessness is not admissible to prove conduct on this particular occasion.
trap_note: A broad character description is different from a specific, regular habit.

setting: A civil trial concerns a disputed loan payment. Counsel offers the borrower's unrelated dishonesty solely to show the borrower must have withheld this payment.

transcript.speaker: Q
transcript.text: How honest is the borrower in everyday life?

transcript.speaker: A
transcript.text: I wouldn't trust her with anything.

explanation: The opinion is offered as forbidden character-to-conduct proof rather than proper witness impeachment.
trap_note: Character evidence has limited permitted uses; this question does not establish one.

setting: A criminal trial concerns a forged ticket. The defendant has offered no character evidence, and the prosecution offers an unrelated lie solely to prove a dishonest disposition.

transcript.speaker: Q
transcript.text: Did the defendant ever lie about winning a competition?

transcript.speaker: A
transcript.text: Yes. He claimed he won when he hadn't even entered.

explanation: The unrelated lie is offered only to suggest dishonest character and therefore guilt.
trap_note: Calling an act dishonest does not supply a proper nonpropensity purpose.

setting: A civil trial concerns damage to a hired canoe. Counsel offers the renter's general recklessness to establish that he caused this particular damage.

transcript.speaker: Q
transcript.text: How would you describe the renter's personality?

transcript.speaker: A
transcript.text: He's reckless about everything.

explanation: General recklessness cannot ordinarily prove conduct in a particular civil incident.
trap_note: This broad personality judgment is not evidence of a specific repeated habit.

setting: A criminal trial concerns an alleged arson. The defendant has not offered character evidence, and the prosecutor offers an unrelated act of cruelty solely to make guilt seem likely.

transcript.speaker: Q
transcript.text: What did the defendant do to a neighbor's garden years ago?

transcript.speaker: A
transcript.text: He tore up the flowers for no reason.

explanation: The unrelated act is offered only to portray bad character and infer criminal conduct.
trap_note: Disapproval of a person's past behavior is not a permitted substitute for proof of the charged offense.

setting: A civil trial concerns a disputed sale of a bicycle. Counsel offers the seller's reputation for greed solely to prove that she overcharged this buyer.

transcript.speaker: Q
transcript.text: What is the seller's reputation where you live?

transcript.speaker: A
transcript.text: People say she's greedy.

explanation: Greedy character is offered to infer conduct in the particular transaction.
trap_note: A reputation witness still needs a legally permissible character issue.

setting: A criminal trial concerns a warehouse break-in. The prosecutor offers a past trespass solely to suggest the defendant is the sort of person who enters property unlawfully.

transcript.speaker: Q
transcript.text: Have you seen the defendant trespass before?

transcript.speaker: A
transcript.text: Yes, he climbed into a closed swimming pool one summer.

explanation: The prior trespass is used only as propensity proof.
trap_note: Prior acts can have permitted uses, but merely showing a tendency to trespass is not one.

setting: A civil trial concerns a bus collision. Counsel offers the driver's general impatience solely to prove that he rushed through the junction.

transcript.speaker: Q
transcript.text: How patient is the driver in ordinary conversations?

transcript.speaker: A
transcript.text: Not at all. He always wants people to hurry up.

explanation: A general personality trait cannot ordinarily prove conduct in this civil accident.
trap_note: Conversational impatience is not a specific routine response to a driving situation.

setting: A criminal trial concerns an alleged robbery. The prosecutor offers an unrelated school disciplinary incident solely to portray the defendant as a troublemaker.

transcript.speaker: Q
transcript.text: Was the defendant punished for disrupting class years ago?

transcript.speaker: A
transcript.text: Yes, for throwing paper across the room.

explanation: The school incident is offered only to invite a bad-character inference.
trap_note: Being a past troublemaker does not prove a charged robbery.

setting: A civil trial concerns whether a tenant damaged a door. Counsel offers a witness's broad view that the tenant is destructive, rather than evidence about the door.

transcript.speaker: Q
transcript.text: What kind of person is the tenant?

transcript.speaker: A
transcript.text: Someone who ruins things wherever he goes.

explanation: The testimony uses general character to infer conduct on the disputed occasion.
trap_note: A sweeping description is not evidence of what happened to this door.

setting: A criminal trial concerns a false expense claim. The prosecution offers an unrelated gambling habit solely to argue that the defendant is morally untrustworthy.

transcript.speaker: Q
transcript.text: Does the defendant spend money at card games?

transcript.speaker: A
transcript.text: Yes, most weekends.

explanation: The offered moral-character inference is not a proper basis for proving this false claim.
trap_note: Disfavored personal activities do not establish guilt through character alone.

setting: A civil trial concerns a missed contractual deadline. Counsel offers the supplier's general laziness solely to prove nonperformance.

transcript.speaker: Q
transcript.text: What is the supplier like as a person?

transcript.speaker: A
transcript.text: Lazy. He never wants to do anything.

explanation: General laziness is used to infer conduct in this particular transaction.
trap_note: The question asks for character, not observations of the work at issue.

setting: A criminal trial concerns a stolen laptop. The defendant has offered no character evidence, and the prosecutor presents a general opinion that the defendant is a thief.

transcript.speaker: Q
transcript.text: What is your opinion of the defendant's character?

transcript.speaker: A
transcript.text: He's a thief at heart.

explanation: The prosecution is using a character opinion to prove the charged theft.
trap_note: An opinion label does not avoid the restriction on propensity evidence.

setting: A civil trial concerns damage to an industrial motor. An untrained office clerk offers a technical diagnosis based only on looking at its casing.

transcript.speaker: Q
transcript.text: What engineering defect caused the motor to fail?

transcript.speaker: A
transcript.text: The rotor must have had a torsional resonance problem.

explanation: The technical engineering diagnosis requires specialized knowledge beyond permissible lay opinion.
trap_note: A witness's personal view of the casing does not qualify a technical diagnosis.

setting: A criminal trial concerns a questioned signature. A witness with no handwriting expertise or prior familiarity offers a forensic conclusion from comparing specimens in court.

transcript.speaker: Q
transcript.text: What does your comparison prove?

transcript.speaker: A
transcript.text: The pressure patterns prove the defendant forged it.

explanation: The proposed forensic analysis depends on specialized knowledge rather than ordinary perception.
trap_note: Looking at two samples does not automatically qualify a witness to give expert handwriting analysis.

setting: A civil trial concerns an illness after chemical exposure. A lay coworker offers a medical diagnosis from seeing the claimant cough.

transcript.speaker: Q
transcript.text: What disease did that cough show?

transcript.speaker: A
transcript.text: It was definitely chemical pneumonitis.

explanation: A medical diagnosis requires specialized knowledge beyond the coworker's lay observations.
trap_note: The witness can describe the cough without diagnosing its medical cause.

setting: A civil trial concerns a cracked foundation. A neighbor with no engineering training assigns a technical structural cause after seeing the crack.

transcript.speaker: Q
transcript.text: Why did the foundation fail?

transcript.speaker: A
transcript.text: Differential soil consolidation exceeded the footing's design tolerance.

explanation: The explanation relies on specialized structural and soil analysis.
trap_note: Seeing a crack permits a description, not an unsupported engineering diagnosis.

setting: A criminal trial concerns an unknown powder. An untrained witness identifies its chemical composition solely from its color.

transcript.speaker: Q
transcript.text: What chemical was in the bag?

transcript.speaker: A
transcript.text: It was fentanyl. I could tell because it was white.

explanation: Identifying chemical composition here requires specialized knowledge rather than an ordinary visual impression.
trap_note: The witness may describe the appearance without supplying an unsupported chemical identification.

setting: A civil trial concerns a failed computer server. A receptionist with no technical background diagnoses the underlying software fault from a blank screen.

transcript.speaker: Q
transcript.text: What caused the outage?

transcript.speaker: A
transcript.text: A race condition in the database's transaction manager.

explanation: The software diagnosis rests on specialized knowledge beyond the witness's perception.
trap_note: Observing a blank screen does not establish the technical mechanism behind it.

setting: A criminal trial concerns a firearm discharge. A lay witness offers a ballistics reconstruction from a hole in a wall without relevant expertise.

transcript.speaker: Q
transcript.text: What angle did the bullet enter at?

transcript.speaker: A
transcript.text: Exactly seventeen degrees downward, based on the hole's shape.

explanation: The precise trajectory analysis requires specialized ballistics knowledge.
trap_note: The witness can describe the hole without calculating an expert trajectory.

setting: A civil trial concerns spoiled medicine. An untrained delivery worker offers a pharmacological conclusion after seeing a package sit in sunlight.

transcript.speaker: Q
transcript.text: What did the sunlight do to the medicine?

transcript.speaker: A
transcript.text: It broke the active molecule into a toxic compound.

explanation: The molecular conclusion requires specialized scientific knowledge.
trap_note: A firsthand observation of sunlight does not establish its chemical effects.

setting: A civil trial concerns a damaged antique clock. A witness with no appraisal experience offers a valuation based on technical rarity classifications.

transcript.speaker: Q
transcript.text: What is the clock worth?

transcript.speaker: A
transcript.text: Forty thousand dollars because its escapement belongs to a rare transitional series.

explanation: This appraisal relies on specialized knowledge not established for the lay witness.
trap_note: An opinion grounded in technical classification is not ordinary lay perception.

setting: A criminal trial concerns a broken lock. A neighbor without locksmith expertise identifies a specific tool from microscopic markings.

transcript.speaker: Q
transcript.text: What tool made those marks?

transcript.speaker: A
transcript.text: A six-pin tubular pick, definitely.

explanation: The specialized tool-mark identification exceeds the witness's ordinary observations.
trap_note: Describing visible scratches is different from identifying their technical source.

setting: A civil trial concerns a speeding van. A witness watched it pass nearby and gives an ordinary estimate based on years of seeing traffic.

transcript.speaker: Q
transcript.text: How fast did it seem to be going?

transcript.speaker: A
transcript.text: Around forty miles an hour. Much faster than the other cars on that street.

explanation: An ordinary speed estimate based on firsthand observation can be helpful lay opinion.
trap_note: Not every numerical estimate requires expert testimony.

setting: A civil trial concerns a visibly intoxicated guest. A server describes an impression grounded in slurred speech and unsteady movement she personally observed.

transcript.speaker: Q
transcript.text: How did the guest seem when he stood up?

transcript.speaker: A
transcript.text: Drunk. He was slurring and had to hold the table to stay upright.

explanation: The impression is grounded in ordinary firsthand observations and helps describe the guest's condition.
trap_note: A lay witness may describe apparent intoxication without a laboratory diagnosis.

setting: A criminal trial concerns an assault. The defendant properly offers a character witness's opinion about the defendant's pertinent trait of peacefulness.

transcript.speaker: Q
transcript.text: From knowing the defendant, what is your opinion of his peacefulness?

transcript.speaker: A
transcript.text: He's a peaceful person. I've known him for twelve years.

explanation: A criminal defendant may offer evidence of a pertinent character trait.
trap_note: The prohibition on propensity evidence has a specific exception for a defendant's pertinent trait.

setting: A civil trial concerns a witness whose truthfulness has been attacked. A qualified reputation witness is called to support that witness's character for truthfulness.

transcript.speaker: Q
transcript.text: What is her reputation for telling the truth in your community?

transcript.speaker: A
transcript.text: She's known as someone who tells the truth, even when it's awkward.

explanation: Truthful-character reputation may be offered after the witness's character for truthfulness has been attacked.
trap_note: Supporting truthful character is limited, but the required attack has occurred here.

setting: A civil trial concerns an employer's routine mail handling. A longtime clerk describes a specific, consistent response to every registered letter rather than a broad personality trait.

transcript.speaker: Q
transcript.text: What happened each time a registered letter arrived?

transcript.speaker: A
transcript.text: I stamped it, entered its number in the ledger, and put it in the locked tray.

explanation: A specific, regular routine may support an inference that the procedure was followed on the occasion at issue.
trap_note: Habit or routine practice differs from a broad character trait such as carefulness.

setting: A civil trial concerns a damaged bicycle. Its owner gives an ordinary description of how it rode immediately after the collision based on personally riding it.

transcript.speaker: Q
transcript.text: How did the bicycle feel when you tried to ride home?

transcript.speaker: A
transcript.text: The front wheel wobbled so badly that I had to walk it.

explanation: The description is a helpful impression grounded in the owner's direct experience.
trap_note: The witness is describing operation, not offering an engineering diagnosis.
